doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: No retirement: musicians who keep playing
summary: They joke about retirement and cite Moody, Elvin Jones and Milt Hinton as examples of music as a life force.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: Well I’m sure both of you guys are putting a lot away towards retirement.

What am I going to retire to? What am I going to retire to? That’s the great thing. I mean I look at James Moody, he’s 76. I talked to Pat LaBarbara today, he’s going to go out and play with Elvin again. You know Elvin is 73. These guys are only getting better. What are they going to do go play golf? I mean they’re still getting better. I mean that’s the great thing about being a musician. It’s like every day I look forward to playing because there’s going to be something different than the day before. I mean I got no pension plan with my job, we’re out there in the real world. Anything we do is IRAs or whatever kind of stuff. It’s like man, I don’t know what I would retire to.
I hate to think what you would retire to, really. I wouldn’t want to be around.
Man. I’m just hoping my mind and body can keep it together.

Yeah but you know that’s the thing about music, like you’re talking about Moody and everybody. If you look at what music can do for you, in terms of years, and you see people that are like 72 years old and they look good and they’re happy, and they’re happy because they’re playing.
And this is their life force.
Look at Milt Hinton, how long was Milt, what was he 90 or something?

I mean man this guy, he just kept going. And he always had a smile on his face, and he brought a great vibe to everybody, and he just kept doing it and I mean he had it together for a long time. I mean he was playing up ‘till he was around 87, 88, right?

If you look at a lot of other people in other lines of work and they have ulcers and they’re stressed out at like 60 and they’re burned out and they’re miserable. It’s a big difference. If you’re the person that finds that they should be playing music to make you happy, you’re not going to play it to get rich. Hopefully you’re going to make an okay living and
all that stuff but if that’s really in you that this is what you do, that can keep you going for a lot of years.

I feel like I’m just starting to get the hang of it now. I really do. I feel like in the past year or so I’m starting to get a clearer idea. I mean this is after doing it a long time. And that’s a great feeling, because it keeps me hungry, keeps me humble, and keeps me like vibrant.
It’s a constant challenge, which is a good thing.
